catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-josaphat-k:
Josaphat Kuncevyc, martyr archbishop of the Ruthenian union, died by axe and bullet at Vitebsk in 1623. Born at Volodymyr in Lithuania in 1580, or 1584 by some writers, he was son of a noble Ruthenian father turned town councillor in commerce. He grew up as the Florentine Union lay dead and the Ruthenian clergy sank into ignorance and vice. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Vitebsk to 12 November 1623.

After Berest's union of 1596, Ruthenians split into Uniates and schismatics, each with its own hierarchy. Meletius Smotryckyj, conspicuous among schismatic leaders, stirred popular hatred against Uniates, and Josaphat became his most celebrated victim. On 12 November 1623 an axe stroke and a bullet gave him a martyr's crown. Urban VIII's commission of 1628 examined 116 witnesses on oath, finding his body still incorrupt five years after death.
doe-osti-2999533-development-of-the-well:
Livia Benvenutti, Christopher Kolodziej, Shashwat Tripathi and co-workers at Argonne National Laboratory describe a new marine fuel model in ANL/ESIA-25/18, built inside R&D GREET 2025. GREET is Argonne's life-cycle accounting tool for transport energy. Well-to-wake scoring follows a ship fuel from production through delivery to the exhaust left behind the vessel, the marine twin of the well-to-wheel view used for road fuels.

Two linked worksheets carry the model. The Marine_Fuel tab lets users pick scenarios and reports energy use, water use and emissions stage by stage for each fuel. The Marine_Trip tab then works out whole voyages for listed vessel types. Together they let analysts compare marine fuel options, from standard fuels to newer low-carbon candidates, on one consistent basis. The report explains inputs, structure and fuel-specific results, so shipping decarbonisation claims can be checked against the same yardstick.
doe-osti-2999900-abstract-for-crada-betw: Scott Crawford and Ryan Stolley's one-page abstract covers a cooperative research agreement, AGMT-1641, between the National Energy Technology Laboratory and GlycoSurf, Incorporated. Rare earth elements are vital to energy and defence technology, yet testing for them is slow and costly. GlycoSurf sells surfactants that pull rare earths out of harsh liquids such as acid mine drainage. The project will add fluorescent groups to those surfactants, so trace rare earths announce themselves by glowing in element-specific bands, even in strong, acidic water.
doe-osti-3024345-techno-economic-feasibi:
Oscar Rosales Calderon and Robert M Baldwin of the National Laboratory of the Rockies. They updated the case for renewable propane in report NLR/TP-5100-98286, dated March 2026, produced for the Propane Education and Research Council. The study weighs techno-economics, feasibility, and life cycle impacts together. Renewable propane rides along with other biofuel processes, so its outlook depends on theirs.

Pathways with high readiness, rated TRL 8 to 9 from demonstration to commercial scale, can already yield significant renewable propane as a by-product, as the HEFA route does. The update also surveys ethanol-to-jet, gasification with Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, and pyrolysis. Sections then turn to feedstock availability, since any route is capped by how much suitable raw material the market can supply.
podcast-joerogan-h4y5o6yH9Yc:
Free will, the Unabomber, and the Harvard LSD studies make a dark triple bill in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rogan ranges across three linked fascinations: whether our choices are truly ours, how a math prodigy became a bomber, and the campus drug tests he passed through first.

The talk follows the thread from Harvard's labs, where Ted Kaczynski was a young subject in harsh mind studies, to the cabin where the manifesto was written. Rogan asks what the tale says about minds pushed by systems. The segment is a grim, gripping triptych, one of the show's deep dives into America's strangest files.
podcast-tuckercarlson-Of3ys0dmyYc:
Father Chad Ripperger is a Catholic priest who casts out demons, one of the most heard in America. He joins Tucker Carlson to discuss possession in public life and occult acts around it. He also discusses his own claimed talks with Satan during rites of exorcism. The interview treats the demonic as a working feature of modern politics, not a metaphor.

Ripperger describes his ministry's caseload and the church's tests for distinguishing possession from illness, then applies his framework to public figures. Carlson receives it as reportage from a hidden front. Listeners outside the faith will find the claims beyond proof by design; listeners inside it will hear a famed priest state what he has seen. The episode preserves exorcism's current public face: credentialed, calm, and entirely convinced, explaining evil's personnel to an audience of millions.
